content.text: The Library is best understood at this stage not as a physical place, an answer space, or a region through which an observer progressively searches, but as the static, maximally complete total configuration domain of the NSFG construction. It is a dimensionally undifferentiated relational totality characterized by closure under the primitive operation \(\oplus\), together with self-containment and the absence of a privileged definable exterior. Closure specifies a mathematical property of the Library; it does not describe a chronological, developmental, or ontological process by which the Library is generated. The Library therefore does not begin in a simple state and become more complex. It is maximally complete at every abstract traversal index. Formally, \(\forall i,\; \mathcal{M}_i = \mathcal{M}\). Apparent succession, increasing complexity, locality, distance, and restriction of possible continuations arise from the observer's changing relation to this unchanged totality.

content.title: Static Totality
content.text: The Library is the static, maximally complete, unbounded relational totality satisfying closure under the primitive distinction operation \(\oplus\), self-containment with respect to the formal resources of the system, and absence of a privileged definable exterior. It is not a physical container, metric space, temporal sequence, generated structure, or singularity.
content.interpretation: The Library is treated as an invariant totality. Any apparent succession belongs to observer-relative traversal rather than to changes in Library membership.

content.title: Static Closure Property
content.text: The Library is closed under the primitive distinction operation.
content.interpretation: Closure is a property of \(\mathcal{M}\). It does not imply that repeated applications of \(\oplus\) temporally construct or generate the Library.

content.text: The closure condition therefore must be read statically. It says that the result of the primitive operation remains within the Library; it does not say that the Library came into existence through successive applications of that operation. Likewise, notation such as \(\mathcal{M}_i\) may be used to represent an observer's changing relational reference at abstract index \(i\), but it does not represent distinct temporal versions of the totality.

content.title: Library Invariance
content.text: The underlying Library remains unchanged across abstract traversal indices.
content.interpretation: Observer state, history, accessibility, distinguishability, and coherent continuation may change while the underlying totality remains invariant.

content.title: Unboundedness
content.text: Unboundedness means that the axiomatic floor imposes no privileged finite boundary, terminal region, coordinate limit, or externally supplied truncation on \(\mathcal{M}\). It does not require a particular cardinality, dimensionality, metric, or physical interpretation.
content.interpretation: The Library has no intrinsic edge at which coherent traversal must terminate merely because of a configuration's location within the totality. Unboundedness describes the absence of an imposed boundary condition rather than a claim that every conceivable mathematical object is necessarily represented.

content.text: Because no coordinate, region, or configuration is privileged as the boundary of \(\mathcal{M}\), any admissible \(x \in \mathcal{M}\) may serve as an observer-relative reference without becoming an ontological origin or boundary. Relocating the observer's reference changes the relation through which configurations are evaluated; it does not relocate, regenerate, or redefine the Library.

content.title: Maximal Completeness
content.text: The Library is maximally complete because no configuration, construction history, reference configuration, coordinate, or worldline is privileged as the universal origin from which the whole must be generated or ordered.
content.interpretation: Maximal completeness removes the need for a privileged starting point while preserving the distinction between the complete totality and any particular observer-relative traversal through it.

content.text: If coherent traversal were fundamentally available only from configurations associated with a privileged construction origin, that origin would constitute a hidden privileged worldline or reference frame. The maximal Library formulation removes this asymmetry by requiring the underlying totality to remain unchanged when the observer-relative reference is changed.

Domain-Neutral Completeness: The Library's maximal completeness is not relative to any particular domain. Physics, AI, finance, and other application domains do not require distinct Libraries or domain-specific axioms at the foundational level. A configuration that is resolvable under an observer-relative resolution relation is already a configuration of the same underlying totality; what changes is the relation by which the observer distinguishes, maintains, accesses, or navigates configurations. A new application domain therefore requires a new observer-relative resolution relation or derived interpretation, not a new ontological extension of \(\mathcal{M}\).

content.title: Domain-Neutral Foundation
content.text: The foundational Library is independent of the application domain through which an observer resolves it.
content.interpretation: This notation expresses equality of the underlying formal Library, not equality of the derived structures, observer resolutions, empirical interpretations, or domain-specific laws that may emerge over it.

content.text: The domain-neutral statement is deliberately stronger than saying that the same mathematical language can be reused. It states that no domain-specific ontology is inserted beneath the observer-relative constructions. Physics may resolve one family of distinctions, an AI system another, and a financial observer another, but the foundational totality is not partitioned into separate ontological Libraries for those applications. Domain differences arise at the level of resolution, accessibility, coherence, persistence, and derived regularity.

This does not mean that physics, AI, and finance are empirically or mathematically identical. Their observers, resolution functions, histories, observables, and derived regularities may differ substantially. Domain neutrality means only that such differences are introduced through observer-relative relations over the same foundational totality rather than through separate domain-specific axioms at the axiomatic floor.

content.title: Membership
content.text: A configuration belongs to the Library by virtue of membership in the complete total configuration domain, not because it is an answer, a coherent continuation, an observable state, or an accessible state.
content.interpretation: Membership precedes all observer-relative filtering.

content.title: Library Membership
content.text: Library membership denotes belonging to the formally defined total configuration domain.
content.interpretation: Membership in \(\mathcal{M}\) is independent of whether an observer can distinguish, maintain, access, or interpret \(x\).

content.text: Thus \(x \in \mathcal{M}\) does not imply persistence, distinguishability, coherence, physicality, observability, or accessibility. Conversely, failure of observer-relative accessibility does not remove a configuration from the Library. In particular, \(x \notin A_O\) does not imply \(x \notin \mathcal{M}\). Inaccessibility is not erasure.

content.title: Unfiltered Totality
content.text: The Library is unfiltered at the axiomatic level. No observer-relative resolution threshold, persistence condition, coherence criterion, accessibility relation, or physical interpretation is applied to determine Library membership.
content.interpretation: These structures are relations over the already complete totality rather than filters that define what the totality contains.

content.text: Coherent and incoherent configurations therefore belong to the same underlying total configuration domain. Coherence does not divide the Library into ontologically real and unreal regions. Instead, coherence specifies which relations and paths can be maintained relative to an observer, its history, its current reference configuration, and its resolution.

content.title: Whole-Library Relationality
content.text: The Library supplies the whole relational domain over which observer-relative paths, coherence, accessibility, distinguishability, and continuation are evaluated.
content.interpretation: The observer is relationally situated with respect to the whole Library rather than receiving a pre-filtered local subset as the ontological substrate of experience.

content.title: Observer-Relative Coherence Relation
content.text: Coherence evaluates a path relative to the observer, relevant history, and current reference configuration.
content.interpretation: Changing \(O\), \(h\), or \(x\) can change the coherence relation without changing the underlying Library \(\mathcal{M}\).

content.text: The observer does not first receive a locally bounded subset of \(\mathcal{M}\) and then search inside that subset. At every abstract traversal step, the observer is relationally situated with respect to the whole Library. Its experienced traversal is nevertheless restricted to the coherent continuations that can be maintained from its current reference, history, and resolution.

At the axiomatic floor, relational availability does not imply intrinsic spatial adjacency. The Library has no primitive metric distance or dimensional coordinate system. Any experienced notion of near, far, local, or remote belongs to a later observer-relative structure.

content.title: Relational Structure
content.text: The Library may be represented relationally as a maximally connected configuration domain in which configurations can stand in formal relation without requiring intrinsic spatial separation.
content.interpretation: A complete-graph analogy can express the absence of intrinsically isolated configurations, but it is representational rather than a claim that graph topology is a physical primitive.

content.title: Foundational Relational Constraints
items: \(\mathcal{M}\) has no intrinsic dimensionality at the axiomatic floor.
No metric or distance function is primitive to \(\mathcal{M}\).
Traversal is not spatial movement through a pre-existing metric space.
Movement-like language denotes ordered maintenance or selection of coherent relations among configurations already contained in \(\mathcal{M}\).
Any experienced separation between configurations belongs to a later observer-relative relational structure.

content.title: Answer Space as a Derived Construction
content.text: The term 'answer space' may be used for an observer-relative subset of configurations or continuations satisfying a particular query, coherence relation, or navigation criterion, but it is not the ontological definition of \(\mathcal{M}\).
content.interpretation: The Library is prior to any particular question. An observer determines which relations are relevant, distinguishable, coherent, accessible, or navigable without determining what exists in the underlying totality.

content.text: This distinction is essential for cross-domain use. An AI system may construct an answer space through one resolution relation; a financial observer may construct another; a physical observer may construct another. None of these derived spaces replaces the Library or requires a new foundational totality. They are observer-relative structures over the same \(\mathcal{M}\).

sections.title: No Exterior, No Privileged Perspective
sections.purpose: Derive the absence of a privileged God's-eye perspective from the closure construction without introducing an additional physical or observational axiom.
sections.poetic_cypher: There is no balcony outside the Library from which the Library can be judged.
sections.cypher_explanation: The Library is defined as the XOR closure of the formal domain D. A perspective that can be described within the same formal machinery is itself representable within D and therefore cannot remain ontologically external to the closure. The metaphor of the balcony denotes a supposedly privileged external standpoint; the formal result is that such a describable standpoint cannot be both external to \(\mathcal{M}\) and represented by the same formal system.

subsections.title: The Exterior Problem
subsections.purpose: Examine whether a configuration or perspective can function as a privileged reference outside the Library, and distinguish the formal impossibility of a privileged external relation from the broader philosophical question of whether something might exist beyond the theory's defined vocabulary.

content.opening: The static-totality interpretation raises a precise reference problem: can there be a privileged perspective from which the Library as a whole is resolved, ordered, or judged while that perspective itself remains external to the relational structure being described? At this stage, an exterior is not defined geometrically or physically. It is defined formally as a proposed configuration or perspective that is both relevant to the description of the Library and claimed to stand outside the Library's relational domain.

definition.text: Let \(\mathcal{M}\) denote the Library. The Library is formally characterized through the closure relation \(\mathcal{M} := \operatorname{Closure}_{D}(\oplus)\), but this closure is not interpreted as a temporal generation process. An external candidate is a proposed configuration or perspective \(\Omega\) satisfying \(\Omega \notin \mathcal{M}\) while simultaneously being invoked as a reference for resolving relations within \(\mathcal{M}\).
mathematics: \(\Omega \text{ is invoked as a reference for relations within } \mathcal{M}\)

argument.statement: Suppose \(\Omega\) is proposed as an external reference capable of resolving or judging the Library as a whole.

If \(\Omega\) is represented as a configuration using the same formal machinery that defines the axiomatic domain, then that representation is part of the formal configuration domain to which the closure construction applies.
If the represented configuration \(\Omega\) is admitted by the primitive operation and is reachable under the closure relation, then the closure places it within the Library.
The proposed configuration can therefore not simultaneously be an internally represented XOR-generable configuration and remain outside the Library.

The important consequence is not that every conceivable exterior is metaphysically impossible, but that an internally represented configuration cannot acquire privileged external status merely by being declared external.
argument.formal_form: \(\Omega \text{ internally represented and XOR-generable} \Rightarrow \Omega \notin \text{a privileged external class}\)

reference_problem.text: The deeper issue is relational rather than merely set-theoretic. A perspective does not become a privileged reference frame simply because it is postulated outside the Library. To resolve distinctions within \(\mathcal{M}\), an external perspective would require a specified relation connecting it to the configurations being resolved. If that relation is not part of the formal system, the perspective contributes no additional internal coherence rule. If the relation is introduced into the formal system, then the relation itself becomes part of the described structure and must be accounted for by the same ontology.
mathematics: \(R_{\Omega} \in \text{axiomatic vocabulary} \Rightarrow \text{the relation is part of the described formal structure}\)

important_distinction.text: This result must not be confused with the claim that nothing can exist beyond the Library in every imaginable philosophical or mathematical sense. The axiomatic floor makes a narrower claim. An object or perspective that is completely undefined within the formal system is simply outside the theory's vocabulary, and no conclusion about its existence is derived. An object or perspective that is represented within the formal machinery, however, cannot be granted a special ontological status merely by labeling it external.

undefined_or_unknowable.description: A proposed object may have no representation within the formal system. In that case, the axiomatic floor makes no derivation concerning its existence, structure, or relation to the Library.
undefined_or_unknowable.formal_status: \(\Omega \text{ undefined in the formal system} \Rightarrow \text{no derivation about } \Omega\)

describable_exterior.description: A proposed exterior that is represented as a configuration using the same formal machinery is no longer available as an unexplained privileged reference. If that configuration is admitted to the XOR-generable domain, it belongs to the Library under the closure characterization.

external_reference_without_relation.description: A perspective may be verbally postulated as external without thereby acquiring a coherence relation to the Library. Without an internally specified relation, it supplies no God's-eye resolver for distinctions within the Library.

content.scope_note: The conclusion is deliberately weaker than a claim that nothing can exist beyond the Library in every imaginable philosophical or mathematical sense. The axiomatic result concerns the availability of a privileged external reference relation. Such a relation cannot be assumed merely by postulating an exterior. It must either remain undefined, in which case the axiomatic floor derives nothing from it, or be represented within the formal structure, in which case it loses its status as an unexplained privileged standpoint.
content.derived_result: A describable XOR-generable configuration cannot remain an unexplained privileged exterior to \(\mathcal{M}\), and an undefined exterior supplies no derived coherence relation to \(\mathcal{M}\). Therefore the axiomatic floor provides no privileged external God's-eye resolver. Reference must instead be established relationally within the formal structure.

subsections.title: No God's-Eye Resolver
subsections.poetic_cipher: The Library has no master lens.
subsections.content: A privileged resolver would be a hypothetical observer-independent rule that determines, for every pair of configurations, whether their distinction is universally resolved. Formally, let U : D × D → {0,1}, where U(x,y)=1 means that the distinction between x and y is resolved by the rule, and U(x,y)=0 means that it is not. Such a rule would assign a single resolution outcome to every pair independently of any observer configuration. The axiomatic floor does not contain such a rule. The sole primitive operation is XOR, defined on the formal domain D. XOR determines whether two operands differ within the Boolean operation itself: a ⊕ b = 1 if and only if a ≠ b. It does not determine whether that distinction is resolvable by an observer, whether the distinction persists, or whether it should count as accessible. Those are additional relations that require additional structure. Therefore U is not derivable merely from the existence and algebraic properties of XOR. In the notation of the axiomatic floor, U ∉ A_N unless U is explicitly introduced as an additional axiom. Introducing U would change the foundational system by supplying a universal resolution predicate that was not present in the original primitive. This distinction is important. XOR establishes difference; it does not establish a universal scale on which every difference must be resolved. A pair of configurations may therefore be distinct under the formal operation while remaining indistinguishable to a particular observer. The absence of U leaves room for resolution to be relational rather than absolute. Accordingly, NSFG permits an observer-relative resolution relation. For an observer O, a later construction may define a relation D_O(x,y) according to O's own resolution capacity. This does not mean that O creates the distinction between x and y. The distinction already exists within the formal configuration domain. Rather, O determines which distinctions remain effectively resolvable relative to its own structural resolution floor. The consequence is not that every observer has an arbitrary private reality. Rather, the axiomatic floor refuses to privilege one resolution rule as universally authoritative. Observer-relative resolution can therefore be introduced without contradicting XOR, provided that the observer and its resolution capacity are themselves defined as downstream structures rather than smuggled into the primitive. The Library consequently has no master lens: there is no axiom at the floor that selects, from outside all observers, which distinctions must count as universally resolved. Any such lens would be additional structure, not a consequence of XOR. The ability to resolve a distinction must therefore belong to the structure doing the resolving. This provides the formal handoff to the subsequent definition of observer-relative distinguishability and the threshold I_N(O).

sections.title: Observer-Relative Resolution
sections.purpose: Introduce the observer and its resolution capacity without making either primitive.
sections.poetic_cipher: The observer is a difference that remains. The boundary of its remaining is its resolution.
sections.cypher_explanation: The first sentence identifies observerhood with persistence of distinguishability rather than with consciousness or intention. The second identifies resolution as the boundary determining which distinctions can remain stably distinguishable for that observer. The formal resolution threshold is introduced only after observerhood has been established structurally.
sections.introduction: The axiomatic floor has so far defined distinction and the closure generated by distinction, but it has not yet specified what it means for a configuration to maintain a distinction. This section introduces the observer without treating observation as a primitive act. An observer is instead derived as a configuration whose structure permits distinctions to persist across successive states. The observer therefore belongs to the Library in the same formal sense as every other configuration. What distinguishes it is not consciousness, intention, or privileged status, but persistence. Once such a structure is identified, a further question becomes unavoidable: which distinctions can that structure actually maintain? This motivates observer-relative resolution.
sections.scope_boundary: At this stage, observerhood is a structural property only. No claim is made that an observer is conscious, biological, intelligent, physical, or capable of intentional measurement. Those interpretations, if introduced later, are downstream of the axiomatic construction.

subsections.title: Observer as a Derived Structure
subsections.purpose: Define observerhood structurally rather than psychologically, establish observer membership in the Library, and defer consciousness and other interpretive properties to downstream theory.
subsections.content:
An observer is not introduced as a new primitive entity. Since the Library is already defined as the XOR closure of the formal domain, any observer must itself be a configuration within that closure. Observerhood is therefore a property of a configuration, not a separate ontological category. Let \(O\) denote a configuration in the Library. We call \(O\) an observer when its structure is capable of maintaining a persistent chain of distinctions across successive states. The word persistent is important: a single distinction does not constitute an observer. Observerhood requires a continuing structure in which distinctions remain available rather than immediately collapsing into indistinguishability. Formally, observerhood is written as: \[
O \in \mathcal{M}
\] and: \[
O \text{ is an observer} \iff O \text{ is a configuration in } \mathcal{M} \text{ containing a persistent chain of resolvable distinctions.}
\] The term resolvable is deliberately structural rather than psychological. It does not mean that \(O\) consciously notices, interprets, or understands a distinction. It means only that the distinction can remain sufficiently differentiated within the structure represented by \(O\). The quantitative boundary governing that distinction has not yet been introduced; it will be defined through the observer-relative threshold \(I_N(O)\) in the following subsection. This distinction prevents observerhood from being smuggled into the axiomatic floor as consciousness. A configuration may satisfy the structural definition of observerhood without possessing any assumed mental state. Consciousness is therefore not required at the axiomatic level. Whether some later physical or cognitive systems instantiate additional properties associated with conscious observation is a separate question and cannot be inferred from the definition alone. The observer is consequently derived from the same ontology as everything else. It is not outside the Library, above the Library, or granted a privileged position within it. It is a configuration whose internal persistence permits distinctions to remain available across a continuing chain. The dependency is therefore: \[
\text{distinction} \;\rightarrow\; \text{persistence} \;\rightarrow\; \text{observerhood}.
\] The construction has not yet supplied a universal rule determining how much distinction is required for persistence. That question belongs to the observer itself. To say that a distinction survives requires a boundary separating distinctions that remain effective from distinctions that fall below the observer's effective resolution.

subsections.formal_status: The membership condition and structural definition are formal constructions from the stated ontology. The absence of a consciousness requirement is a scope constraint on the axiomatic system, not a claim that consciousness is impossible or irrelevant in downstream theories.
subsections.poetic_cypher: An observer is a difference that survives long enough to have another difference.
subsections.cypher_explanation: A difference represents a distinction. Surviving represents persistence across successive states. Having another difference represents the continuation of distinguishable structure. The cipher therefore compresses observerhood as a persistent structure without introducing consciousness, intention, or any privileged observer.
subsections.handoff: To say that a distinction survives, we must specify the boundary at which a distinction remains effective for the structure that carries it. That boundary is observer-relative resolution, represented by \(I_N(O)\).

content.opening: Once observerhood has been defined as a persistent capacity to maintain distinctions, the next question is not whether distinctions exist in the Library, but which distinctions a particular observer can maintain as stable distinctions. This requires a resolution threshold. The Noor-Planck threshold, written I_N(O), is introduced here as an observer-relative structural quantity. It does not describe a limit imposed by the Library itself, nor does it determine which configurations belong to the Library. It describes the minimum effective distinction that observer O can preserve as a stable distinction within its own configuration.

The naming convention is intended to honor the structural role of a fundamental resolution limit, not to claim a numerical identity with the Planck scale. Any such identity, if it exists, must be derived downstream.

content.text: The important point is the placement of the argument O. Writing I_N(O) makes explicit that resolution is relative to the observer whose capacity to maintain distinctions is being evaluated. Two observers may therefore occupy the same Library 𝓜 while maintaining different effective resolutions. This difference concerns their respective capacities to maintain distinctions; it does not imply that the underlying Library differs between them.

I_N(O) is also domain-neutral at the foundational level. The structural quantity does not become a different axiom when the observer is instantiated in a different domain. In a physical context, I_N(O) may be associated with a scale related to physical resolution; in an AI context, it may represent the effective resolution of a symbolic reasoning system; in a financial context, it may represent a minimum actionable distinction such as a price movement. These are domain-specific interpretations of the same structural quantity, not different foundational thresholds.

No universal numerical value is supplied. In particular, the foundational definition does not identify I_N(O) with the Planck scale, a cognitive limit, a market tick, or any other domain-specific quantity. Such identifications, where useful, must be derived or justified within the corresponding downstream domain.

subsections.title: I_N(O) Is Not a Property of the Library
subsections.content: The Library is a static totality characterized formally through the closure of the formal domain under XOR. This closure notation specifies the mathematical structure of the Library; it does not describe a temporal process by which the Library is progressively generated. Library membership is therefore independent of whether a particular observer can distinguish or maintain a given distinction. Nothing in the axiomatic floor supplies a universal minimum distinction magnitude for the totality itself.
mathematics: I_N(O) \text{ is observer-indexed and is not defined as a universal resolution constant of } \mathcal{M}.
subsections.explanation: A distinction may therefore exist within \mathcal{M} without being stably resolvable by O. If observer O cannot maintain a distinction because its magnitude lies below I_N(O), that limitation changes the observer's effective description of the relation. It does not remove either configuration from the Library, alter Library membership, or collapse the underlying totality. The observer's resolution floor changes what can be maintained as a distinction, not what exists in \mathcal{M}.
subsections.poetic_cypher: The eye closes before the Library does.
subsections.cypher_explanation: Loss of distinction is a property of the observer's resolution, not deletion from the totality. The Library remains unchanged even when a distinction falls below the observer's effective resolution.

subsections.title: Observer Variability
subsections.content: Because the threshold is indexed to observer structure, different observers may have different resolution floors. The axiomatic floor permits this variability rather than imposing equality between observers.
mathematics: \exists O_1,O_2 \in \mathrm{Obs} \text{ such that } I_N(O_1) \neq I_N(O_2) \text{ is permitted.}
subsections.explanation: This does not mean that every arbitrary threshold assignment is valid. Each I_N(O) is intended to characterize the structural capacity of the corresponding observer to maintain distinctions. The threshold is therefore observer-relative without being a freely chosen parameter. Two observers can relate to the same unchanged Library while maintaining different effective resolutions of that Library.
subsections.poetic_cypher: Two hands may hold different rulers, yet each ruler still has a length.
subsections.cypher_explanation: Different observers may have different resolution floors, but each threshold remains a definite structural quantity for the observer to which it belongs. Observer relativity therefore does not imply arbitrariness.

subsections.title: No Universal Threshold Is Assumed
subsections.content: The axiomatic floor does not assert the existence of a single threshold shared by every observer. Nor does it require the negation of such a universal value. The present construction simply leaves universality unestablished unless it is derived from additional structure.
mathematics: \forall O \in \mathrm{Obs},\ I_N(O) = I_N^* \text{ is not an axiom of the present construction.}
\exists I_N^*\ \forall O \in \mathrm{Obs},\ I_N(O) = I_N^* \text{ may be investigated only as a derived or additional result.}
subsections.explanation: This distinction preserves the logical scope of the axiomatic floor. A universal threshold and an observer-relative threshold make different commitments, but the absence of a universal axiom is not itself a proof that no universal value could ever emerge. A later theory may derive a common scale, identify conditions under which observer thresholds converge, or demonstrate that they remain distinct. None of those possibilities is assumed here.
subsections.poetic_cypher: One floor is not built into the whole Library; each structure stands on its own threshold.
subsections.cypher_explanation: The present axioms assign the resolution floor to the observer rather than to the Library as a universal law. Whether a deeper derivation produces a common scale remains an open downstream question.

subsections.title: Relative Does Not Mean Arbitrary
subsections.content: Calling I_N(O) observer-relative does not make distinguishability a matter of arbitrary preference. The observer is itself a configuration in the Library, and its threshold is intended to be determined by the structural capacity of that configuration to maintain distinctions. Thus the threshold is relative to a particular observer while remaining constrained by the structure of that observer.
mathematics: I_N(O) = \text{the structural resolution floor associated with the distinction-maintenance capacity of } O.
subsections.explanation: The distinction is therefore between relativity and arbitrariness. Relative means that the value is indexed to the observer under consideration. Arbitrary would mean that the value could be assigned without regard to the observer's structure. The axiomatic construction requires the former and does not imply the latter. The threshold belongs to the observer-relative relation between a configuration and the distinctions that configuration can maintain; it does not become a new ontological boundary inside the Library.
subsections.poetic_cypher: The measure follows the measurer, not the world.
subsections.cypher_explanation: The observer's resolution determines the distinctions that can be maintained by that observer. It does not determine the contents, membership, or completeness of the Library.

content.formal_conclusion: The introduction of I_N(O) establishes an observer-relative resolution condition without making resolution an ontological filter on the Library. The static totality \mathcal{M} remains unchanged regardless of the resolution of a particular observer. A distinction may therefore belong to \mathcal{M} while remaining below the effective resolution of O. Different observers may possess different resolution floors, and no universal value of I_N is assumed at the axiomatic level. The resulting separation is foundational: Library membership concerns what belongs to \mathcal{M}; observer-relative resolution concerns what O can maintain as a distinction. The next construction can therefore distinguish ontological membership from observer-relative distinguishability, accessibility, and ultimately coherence without allowing any of those relations to shrink or redefine the totality.
content.handoff: With the observer-specific resolution floor established independently of Library membership, the next section can formalize the difference between a distinction that exists within \mathcal{M} and a distinction that observer O can resolve and maintain.
content.poetic_cypher: The eye closes before the Library does.
content.cypher_explanation: The resolution threshold belongs to the observer's capacity rather than to the Library as a universal law. What falls below the observer's resolution is not erased from the totality; it simply ceases to function as a maintained distinction for that observer.

sections.title: Persistence and the Birth of the Observer
sections.purpose: Formalize survivable distinctions and derive observerhood as persistent structure.
sections.poetic_cypher: A distinction that can be kept is a distinction that can persist. A structure that persists its distinctions becomes an observer.
sections.cypher_explanation: The section moves from primitive XOR distinction through observer-relative magnitude evaluation and resolution toward persistence and observerhood as derived structural properties. No consciousness, intention, agency, or human perception is required. An observer is introduced only as a configuration capable of maintaining distinctions that remain resolvable above its own observer-specific threshold I_N(O) across an ordered sequence of transitions.

section.title: Distinguishability Relative to O
section.purpose: Define observer-relative distinguishability from the XOR-derived distinction relation while separating operational resolution from ontological membership in the static Library.
section.poetic_cipher: The distance between two points is not measured by a ruler; it is the distinctions required to walk between them.
section.cipher_explanation: The ruler represents an externally imposed metric. The primitive XOR operation supplies the underlying distinction, while the observer-relative magnitude evaluation mu_O determines how that distinction is operationally resolved. No independent external metric is imported into the axiomatic floor.

content.text: The distance between two points is not measured by a ruler; it is the distinctions required to walk between them.

The Library is a static totality whose membership is not determined by any particular observer's resolution. Every configuration considered here is already a member of \(\mathcal{M}\). The question is therefore not whether an observer causes a configuration to exist, but whether the observer can maintain a distinction between configurations at its available resolution. Once the observer-specific threshold \(I_N(O)\) is introduced, distinguishability becomes relational: the same pair of configurations may be operationally distinguishable to one observer while falling below the resolution threshold of another. This difference belongs to the observer-relative relation, not to the ontological membership of the configurations.

content.title: XOR-Derived Distinction
content.text: Let \(x,y\in\mathcal{M}\). Define the XOR-derived distinction relation as the minimum number of XOR operations required to relate \(x\) and \(y\) through configurations contained in \(\mathcal{M}\).
content.latex: d_{\oplus}(x,y)=\min\left\{n\in\mathbb{N}_0\mid\exists z_0,\ldots,z_n\in\mathcal{M},\ z_0=x,\ z_n=y,\ \forall i<n,\ \exists w_i\in\mathcal{M}:z_{i+1}=z_i\oplus w_i\right\}
content.interpretation: This grounds the initial distinction relation in the sole primitive operation rather than importing an independent metric. At the Boolean floor, the construction is intentionally minimal and collapses to a discrete 0/1 relation.

content.title: Boolean XOR Floor
content.text: For primitive Boolean XOR, the minimum-operation construction collapses to a discrete relation.
content.interpretation: If \(x\neq y\), then choosing \(w=x\oplus y\) gives \(x\oplus w=y\). Thus one XOR operation is sufficient for every distinct pair. This is an important boundary condition: primitive XOR derives distinction, but does not by itself supply a rich continuous metric.

content.text: The Boolean XOR floor is a boundary condition that must not be overlooked. Primitive XOR supplies a single-step distinction relation because any distinct pair can be related in one XOR operation: \(x\oplus(x\oplus y)=y\). Consequently, primitive XOR alone does not provide a meaningful multi-step distance or continuous metric geometry. Any such structure requires additional downstream construction, such as multi-step composition, weighted distinctions, or domain-specific interpretation of \(\mu_O\). The foundation is intentionally minimal; richer geometry belongs to later NSFG work.

The distinction relation therefore has two layers that must not be conflated. The first is the XOR-derived structural distinction supplied by the axiomatic floor. The second is the observer-relative effective evaluation of that distinction. The latter determines how strongly the primitive distinction is resolved by a particular observer. A richer magnitude, including any multi-step or geometric interpretation, requires additional structure beyond primitive Boolean XOR and must therefore be introduced explicitly rather than silently imported.

content.title: Observer-Relative Magnitude Evaluation
content.text: Let \(O\) be an observer. Define \(\mu_O\) as the observer-relative magnitude evaluation function that maps a primitive XOR distinction to an effective magnitude resolvable by observer \(O\). The function is monotonic with respect to the primitive XOR distinction, while its specific functional form remains unspecified at the foundational level.
content.interpretation: The function \(\mu_O\) is the observer's mode of evaluating the distinction supplied by XOR. It is not an externally supplied ruler, universal metric, or additional primitive. Its domain-neutral formal role is fixed here; its specific realization may be supplied by a downstream observer structure or domain-specific interpretation.

content.title: Monotonicity of Observer-Relative Evaluation
content.text: The observer-relative magnitude evaluation preserves the ordering supplied by the primitive Boolean distinction.
content.latex: x\oplus y=1\ \land\ u\oplus v=0\ \Rightarrow\ \mu_O(x\oplus y)\geq\mu_O(u\oplus v)
content.interpretation: A primitive distinction is not evaluated as weaker than the absence of distinction under the same observer-relative evaluation. No stronger numerical structure is assumed.

content.title: Observer-Relative Distinguishability Magnitude
content.text: Let \(O\) be an observer and let \(x,y\in\mathcal{M}\). Define \(\delta_O(x,y)\) as the observer-relative effective distinction magnitude obtained by applying \(\mu_O\) to the primitive XOR distinction \(x\oplus y\).
content.interpretation: The effective distinction is now explicitly grounded in the sole primitive. No independent metric is introduced. Observer dependence enters through \(\mu_O\), while operational resolution is subsequently determined by \(I_N(O)\).

content.title: Observer Resolution Threshold
content.text: The observer-specific threshold \(I_N(O)\) is the minimum effective distinction magnitude that observer \(O\) can maintain as a stable distinction.
content.interpretation: The threshold belongs to the observer. It is not a universal constant and no universal numerical value is supplied by the axiomatic floor.

content.title: Observer-Relative Indistinguishability
content.text: Two configurations are observer-relative indistinguishable when their effective distinction falls below the observer's resolution threshold.
content.interpretation: The relation \(\approx_O\) describes what observer \(O\) can operationally resolve; it does not identify the configurations ontologically.

content.title: Observer-Relative Distinguishability
content.text: Two configurations are observer-relative distinguishable when their effective distinction reaches or exceeds the observer's threshold.
content.interpretation: The threshold is inclusive on the distinguishable side. A distinction exactly equal to \(I_N(O)\) is resolvable by \(O\).

content.text: Because the threshold is indexed by \(O\), resolution is explicitly relational rather than universal. It is permitted that \(I_N(O_1)\neq I_N(O_2)\), and consequently that the same pair \((x,y)\) is distinguishable to \(O_1\) while being indistinguishable to \(O_2\). Nothing about this difference requires the configurations themselves to have changed. Only the observer-relative resolution relation has changed.

content.title: Non-Erasure
content.text: Observer-relative indistinguishability does not imply ontological identity or removal from the Library.
content.interpretation: Two configurations may occupy the same effective resolution class for an observer while remaining distinct configurations of the static Library.

content.title: Membership Preservation
content.text: Observer-relative resolution does not determine Library membership.
content.latex:
x\approx_O y
ot\Rightarrow x
otin\mathcal{M}\qquad	ext{and}\qquad y\approx_O x
ot\Rightarrow y
otin\mathcal{M}
content.interpretation: Failure to resolve a distinction is not erasure. Both configurations may remain members of \(\mathcal{M}\) regardless of whether observer \(O\) can distinguish them.

content.text: Two distinct relations must therefore remain separate. Library membership is a structural fact within the formal model: \(x\in\mathcal{M}\). Observer-relative distinguishability is an operational relation: whether \(O\) can maintain the distinction between \(x\) and \(y\) above \(I_N(O)\). Observer-relative accessibility is consequently a relation over the Library rather than a criterion that determines which configurations belong to it.

content.setup: Suppose \(x,y\in\mathcal{M}\) with \(x\neq y\), and suppose their effective distinction for observer \(O\) satisfies \(\delta_O(x,y)<I_N(O)\).
content.result: Observer \(O\) cannot maintain the difference between \(x\) and \(y\) as a resolved distinction, so \(x\approx_O y\). Nevertheless, \(x\) and \(y\) remain distinct members of the static Library.
content.interpretation: A different observer \(O'\) may resolve the same pair if its magnitude evaluation or resolution threshold differs. Observer-relative resolution therefore changes the accessible description without changing the underlying totality.

content.text: Observer-relative distinguishability may consequently induce resolution classes: configurations whose effective distinctions fall below \(I_N(O)\) can be grouped together operationally for observer \(O\). These classes describe the observer's effective resolution and must not be reified as ontological partitions of \(\mathcal{M}\). The underlying Library remains unchanged while the observer's operational description varies.

The observer's relational reference is likewise not a privileged origin. An observer may evaluate distinctions from a particular configuration or history, but that reference does not establish a boundary around \(\mathcal{M}\), generate the Library, or determine which configurations exist. The whole Library remains the unchanged domain over which observer-relative distinctions are evaluated.

content.title: Foundational Boundary on Distance
content.text: Primitive XOR derives distinction but does not, by itself, determine a rich metric geometry.
content.interpretation: Any later construction of multi-step distance, geometric magnitude, or physical metric must be explicitly derived from additional structure. This prevents an undeclared metric from entering the axiomatic floor.

content.text: The result is a clean separation between distinction, observer-relative evaluation, resolution, and membership. XOR supplies the primitive distinction. The observer-relative function \(\mu_O\) evaluates that distinction, producing \(\delta_O\). The observer-specific threshold \(I_N(O)\) determines whether the evaluated distinction is operationally resolvable. The Library supplies the unchanged totality in which the configurations already reside. None of these layers requires the observer to create reality, and none permits sub-threshold resolution to be interpreted as ontological disappearance.

section.title: Persistence Across Successive Distinctions and Observer-Relative Coherence
section.purpose: Extend single-transition distinguishability into a persistent sequence, establish observerhood as a structural capacity rather than a primitive, and prepare the formal transition from persistence to coherence as an observer-, history-, and reference-relative relation over the unchanged Library.

Its structure is domain-neutral, while its interpretation depends on the domain. In physics the chain may describe worldline continuity; in AI it may describe symbolic coherence across reasoning steps; in finance it may describe persistence of a trend across market states.

content.text: A chain is a chain in physics, in mind, and in markets; only the links differ.

The chain represents persistence: successive distinctions remain resolvable across an ordered sequence. The structure is domain-neutral, while the meaning of each configuration and distinction is domain-specific. The same formal relation can therefore describe physical continuity, symbolic continuity in AI, or trend persistence in finance without treating those domains as different foundational ontologies.

Let \\gamma=(x_0,x_1,\\ldots,x_n) be a finite sequence of configurations in \\mathcal{M}. The index i supplies an abstract ordering of successive configurations. It is not identified with physical time, and the sequence does not represent the progressive creation of Library states.

Every x_i belongs to the same unchanged Library \\mathcal{M}. Traversal through the sequence therefore describes a relation among configurations already contained in the static totality. The Library does not acquire new members as the sequence advances, nor does a prior configuration become absent because a later configuration is traversed.

content.text: Persistence is not a guarantee of continuity in the physical sense; it is a structural property of observer-relative traversal. In physical domains, persistence may correspond to worldline continuity. In AI domains, it may correspond to symbolic coherence across reasoning steps. In financial domains, it may correspond to trend persistence across market states. The structural definition is the same; the interpretation is domain-specific.

This domain-neutrality is a constraint on interpretation, not a claim that physics, AI, and finance contain the same objects or obey the same empirical laws. The commonality lies at the formal level: in each case, persistence concerns the maintenance of resolvable successive distinctions relative to an observer structure and its resolution condition.

content.text: Nothing in this definition requires consciousness, perception, intention, agency, or a human subject. Observerhood names a structural capacity to preserve distinguishability across an abstractly ordered sequence. A human observer may instantiate such a structure, but the formal definition does not privilege humans or conscious systems.

The identification of an observer does not represent a physical birth event or a temporal transition in the Library. It is a structural designation made within the static totality. Wherever the relevant persistent distinguishability structure exists, observer-capable relational structure can be identified without introducing an additional ontological event.

The observer established by persistent distinguishability is not thereby confined to a locally generated region of \\mathcal{M}. Subsequent observer-relative coherence is evaluated over paths in the whole Library. The observer's history and current relational reference can change the resulting accessibility relation while leaving the underlying totality unchanged.

content.interpretation: The continuation set is a relationally selected subset of whole-Library paths. Non-selected paths remain represented in the Library and are not ontologically deleted.

content.text: Under the combined NSFG structural assumptions, every admissible observer-relative reference configuration is required to admit at least one coherent continuation above the relevant observer-dependent coherence floor. This requirement is deliberately stated as a derived structural condition of the combined model rather than as a theorem obtained from maximality alone.

content.interpretation: The condition ensures that admissible observer-relative traversal does not terminate merely because of the coordinate of the current reference within the unbounded Library. It does not assert that every possible path is coherent.

content.text: Persistence therefore supplies the bridge from isolated distinguishability to observerhood. Once persistent distinguishability identifies an observer-capable structure, coherence can be defined as the observer-relative evaluation of paths through the unchanged whole Library. The observer, relevant history, and current relational reference determine the relation; none of them changes the underlying totality.

content.text: Coherence is introduced only after distinguishability, persistence, observerhood, observer-relative resolution, and observer-relative magnitude evaluation have been established. The axiomatic floor therefore does not begin by assigning a universal coherence value to configurations or paths. Instead, coherence is derived from a prior question: does a given transition remain distinguishable to a particular observer O at that observer's available resolution?

The distinction is essential. A path is not coherent or incoherent in itself. The same transition may be resolvable by one observer and unresolved by another if their distinguishability functions or resolution thresholds differ. Coherence is consequently written as a relation between a path and an observer, 𝓒(γ|O), rather than as an observer-independent property 𝓒(γ).

The observer-relative magnitude evaluation μ_O is the source of domain-specific interpretation. In a physical domain, μ_O may be interpreted as a resolution scale related to measurement precision; in an AI domain, as a symbolic distinctness threshold; in a financial domain, as a minimum actionable distinction. The structural relation 𝓒_O remains unchanged; only the interpretation of μ_O and I_N(O) varies.

This construction preserves a strict separation between foundational structure and domain-specific interpretation. The mathematical relation does not specify whether the persistent distinction represents a physical transition, a symbolic reasoning step, or a change in a financial state. Those meanings enter through the observer-relative evaluation μ_O and resolution floor I_N(O), together with downstream domain-specific interpretation. No separate foundational ontology is required for each domain.

At this stage, coherence is deliberately defined as a threshold relation rather than as a physical field, probability, force, or dynamical quantity. The required ingredients are already available: the observer-relative distinguishability function δ_O, the observer-relative resolution threshold I_N(O), and the elementary threshold function Θ. No additional physical axiom is required to establish the relation.

The resulting criterion is binary. A transition either remains resolvable at the observer's threshold or it does not. If two observers possess different resolution thresholds or resolve distinctions differently, the same transition may therefore be coherent for one observer and incoherent for another. This is not a contradiction because coherence was never defined as an absolute property of the transition.

Observer dependence does not mean that the observer creates the underlying configurations or determines whether they belong to the Library. Membership in 𝓜 remains a statement about the formal totality. Coherence instead determines whether a distinction between configurations survives as an observer-maintainable relation at the resolution available to O.

This distinction also preserves the separation between existence and accessibility. A transition that fails the coherence criterion for O is not thereby removed from 𝓜. It simply fails to remain accessible to that observer under the defined resolution condition. Coherence is therefore a relational filter on traversal, not an erasure rule for configurations.

The cross-domain character of this construction is deliberate. The same formal relation may describe traversal through physical, symbolic, computational, financial, or other domain representations. The relational structure is unchanged; what changes is the interpretation assigned to μ_O and I_N(O), and consequently to the observer-relative distinction represented by δ_O.

The distinction between transition coherence and path coherence must also be preserved. A single coherent transition does not establish that an entire path is coherent. A path contains a sequence of transitions, and each transition must independently satisfy the observer-relative coherence condition. Section 7.1 therefore establishes the elementary transition relation before the construction is extended to complete paths.

content.text: Let O be an observer-like configuration and let x_i and x_{i+1} be two successive configurations in an abstractly ordered sequence. By the preceding construction, the effective distinction between these configurations as resolved by O is represented by δ_O(x_i,x_{i+1}), while the minimum effective distinction that O can maintain as a stable distinction is represented by I_N(O).

The effective distinction δ_O is not primitive. It is obtained by applying the observer-relative magnitude evaluation μ_O to the primitive XOR distinction. Thus the transition-level coherence relation remains downstream of the sole foundational distinction operation rather than introducing a new primitive notion of difference.

content.title: Observer Dependence
content.text: The same transition may be coherent relative to one observer and incoherent relative to another.
content.interpretation: Different observers may possess different resolution thresholds or distinguishability functions, so coherence is not an absolute property of the transition.

content.text: If two observers O_1 and O_2 possess different resolution thresholds or magnitude evaluations, then the same transition may satisfy δ_{O_1}(x_i,x_{i+1}) ≥ I_N(O_1) while simultaneously satisfying δ_{O_2}(x_i,x_{i+1}) < I_N(O_2). In that case, the transition is coherent relative to O_1 but not coherent relative to O_2. Nothing contradictory has occurred: coherence was never defined as an absolute property of the transition.

This observer dependence is also the point at which domain-specific interpretation enters the otherwise domain-neutral structure. In a physical domain, μ_O may represent an observer-relative resolution scale associated with measurement precision. In an AI domain, it may represent symbolic distinctness relevant to maintaining a reasoning state. In a financial domain, it may represent a minimum actionable distinction between market states. The structural relation 𝓒_O is unchanged; the interpretation of μ_O and I_N(O) varies with the observer and domain.

The observer dependence of coherence does not mean that the observer creates the underlying configurations or determines whether they belong to the Library. Membership in 𝓜 remains independent of the observer-relative resolution relation. Coherence instead determines whether the distinction between successive configurations remains accessible to O under the specified resolution condition.

The role of I_N(O) is therefore that of a resolution floor. It determines the boundary between distinctions that O can maintain and distinctions that fall below O's effective resolution. No universal numerical value is assigned to I_N(O), and no identification with the ordinary Planck scale is made at this foundational stage.

The foundational XOR operation is Boolean, so no continuous physical metric is implied by the primitive distinction itself. Any effective magnitude represented by μ_O is a downstream observer-relative evaluation of the XOR-derived distinction. Consequently, the existence of δ_O does not introduce a universal continuous geometry at the axiomatic floor.

A single coherent transition does not establish that an entire path is coherent. A path contains a sequence of transitions, and each transition must independently satisfy the observer-relative coherence condition. The next construction therefore extends 𝓒_O from an individual transition to the coherence of an entire path.

content.text: Coherence is defined here as a property of the relation between a path and an observer, not as an intrinsic property of the path alone. Let a path be an abstract finite sequence of configurations \(\gamma=(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), where each \(x_i\in\mathcal{M}\). The sequence index \(i\) denotes abstract ordering only; it is not yet physical time.
content.definition: For an observer \(O\), let the coherence of each transition be defined by \(\mathcal{C}_O(x_i,x_{i+1})=\Theta\!\left(\delta_O(x_i,x_{i+1})-I_N(O)\right)\). Path coherence is then the product of the coherence of every transition along the path:
content.interpretation: Because each factor is either 0 or 1, the product is 1 exactly when every transition in the path remains resolvable by observer \(O\). If even one transition falls below the observer's resolution threshold \(I_N(O)\), the corresponding factor is 0 and the path is incoherent for that observer.
content.observer_dependence: This definition makes observer dependence explicit. Two observers may assign different coherence values to the same path because their resolution thresholds and effective distinguishability functions may differ. Thus, for observers \(O_1\) and \(O_2\), it is permitted that \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O_1)\neq\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O_2)\). A path can therefore be coherent for one observer while being incoherent for another without any contradiction.
content.no_universal_coherence: There is consequently no universal coherence constant supplied by the axiomatic floor. Coherence is not a fixed scalar belonging to \(\gamma\) independently of its observer. The meaningful foundational object is the relation \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)\): the coherence of path \(\gamma\) relative to observer \(O\). Any later theory that assigns a universal numerical coherence parameter would require additional axioms and cannot be inferred from the present construction alone.
content.formal_consequence: The distinction is important because the Library itself remains unfiltered. A path for which \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)=0\) has not been removed from \(\mathcal{M}\). It has merely failed the coherence condition relative to that observer. Coherence therefore determines accessibility rather than ontological membership.
content.boundary: At this stage, coherence does not describe physical stability, causal consistency, energetic feasibility, or any other physical law. It describes only whether the successive distinctions along a path remain resolvable relative to a specified observer.
content.poetic_cipher: The same road may be solid beneath one traveler and vanish beneath another.
content.cipher_explanation: The road represents the path \(\gamma\). Its being solid represents \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)=1\), meaning that every transition remains resolvable for the observer. Its vanishing represents \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)=0\), meaning that at least one transition falls below the observer's resolution threshold. Different travelers represent different observers with potentially different resolution capacities. The metaphor therefore expresses observer-relative coherence without introducing an additional primitive.
content.handoff: If coherence is relational, then each observer traverses only a subset of the Library through paths that remain coherent relative to that observer. This motivates the next construction: the observer-accessible subset \(A_O\subseteq\mathcal{M}\), which provides the formal basis for observer-accessible reality.

content.text: The Library, 𝓜, is defined at the axiomatic floor as the XOR closure of the generating configurations within the formal domain D. Its membership is therefore determined by the formal characterization of the totality: a configuration either belongs to 𝓜 or it does not. The closure relation is mathematical rather than temporal. It does not describe a process by which the Library is progressively generated, expanded, or traversed into existence.

Observer-relative accessibility introduces a different question. Rather than asking whether a configuration belongs to the Library, we ask whether that configuration occurs within a path whose distinctions remain resolvable by a particular observer O. Accessibility therefore concerns the relation between an observer and the unchanged totality. It is not a second membership criterion.

content.title: Observer-Relative Accessibility
content.text: For observer O, relevant history h, and admissible reference configuration x, A_O(h,x) is the subset of 𝓜 containing configurations that occur on at least one path beginning from (h,x) whose transitions remain coherent relative to O.
content.latex: A_O(h,x) = \{y \in \mathcal{M} \mid \exists \gamma \in \operatorname{Path}(\mathcal{M})\text{ beginning at }(h,x)\text{ and containing }y\text{ such that }\mathcal{C}(\gamma \mid O,h,x)=1\}
content.interpretation: The accessible subset is determined by coherent traversal relative to the observer, its relevant history, and its current relational reference. It is not generated by the observer.

content.text: The distinction between membership and accessibility is fundamental. The condition y ∈ 𝓜 concerns the formal status of y within the static totality. The condition y ∈ A_O(h,x) concerns whether y can be reached through a coherent observer-relative traversal from the specified history and reference. These conditions are therefore not equivalent.

content.title: Non-Erasure
content.text: Failure of accessibility does not imply failure of Library membership.
content.interpretation: A configuration may remain fully contained within 𝓜 while being inaccessible to a particular observer under a particular relational condition.

content.text: The Library is consequently not reduced when an observer has access to only a restricted subset. The observer's resolution, history, and relational reference determine which distinctions can participate in a coherent traversal, while 𝓜 remains unchanged. The observer does not bring inaccessible configurations into existence by resolving them, nor does failure to resolve a configuration remove it from 𝓜.

This also establishes a domain-neutral interpretation of accessibility. A_O(h,x) is the subset of the Library accessible to observer O under its current relational conditions. In a physical domain, this may correspond to an observer-accessible set of physical configurations or observable states. In an AI domain, it may correspond to the knowledge or reasoning context available to a system. In a financial domain, it may correspond to the set of actionable market states available under the observer's current informational and relational conditions. The structural definition is the same; only the interpretation of what counts as accessible content changes.
The same window frames a star, a thought, and a price; the frame is the same.

The 'window' represents A_O(h,x). The 'star', 'thought', and 'price' represent physical, AI, and financial domains. The structural accessibility relation is the same across domains; its interpreted contents differ.

This domain neutrality does not require the accessible subsets of different observers or domains to be identical. It states only that the formal relation is invariant: accessibility is evaluated as an observer-relative relation over the same Library structure. Domain-specific meaning enters through the interpretation of configurations, observer state, resolution, history, and actionable continuation, not through a new foundational ontology.

content.title: Experienced Reality
content.text: For the purposes of the primer, observer-relative experienced reality is identified with the accessible subset of the Library.
content.interpretation: R_O(h,x) names the portion of the unchanged Library available through coherent traversal relative to observer O, history h, and reference x. This notation does not identify the accessible subset with the whole Library.

content.text: The observer is therefore relationally situated with respect to the whole Library rather than ontologically confined to a local region of it. Observer-relative locality belongs to the traversal relation, not to an intrinsic partition of 𝓜. A change of observer, history, resolution, or admissible reference may change the accessible relation without changing the underlying totality.

No intrinsic past/future partition is introduced into 𝓜 at this stage. A sequence of configurations encountered by an observer supplies an ordering of traversal relative to its history and reference. Apparent temporal sequence therefore belongs to the observer-relative relation over the Library rather than to an ontological evolution of the Library itself.

Likewise, an observer may experience increasing complexity, locality, or differentiation as its relational history changes, but this does not imply that 𝓜 itself evolves from simpler to more complex states. The totality remains unchanged while the observer's relation to it changes.

At this stage, A_O(h,x) is a formal construction describing observer-relative accessibility within the Library. It is not identified directly with human sensory experience, phenomenal consciousness, a complete physical universe, or any other specific physical ontology.

The first relation concerns the static totality; the second concerns the observer's relation to that totality.

content.title: Admissible Reference Configuration
content.text: Let x be a configuration in 𝓜 capable of instantiating an observer-relative reference state under the model's admissibility conditions.
content.interpretation: The reference configuration supplies the relational origin for evaluating accessibility. It is not an ontological origin or generator of 𝓜.

content.text: The observer is relationally situated with respect to the whole Library 𝓜 rather than ontologically confined to a local region of it. The reference x therefore identifies where the observer-relative evaluation begins, not a place where the Library itself begins.

content.title: Reference-Frame Neutrality
content.text: Any two admissible reference configurations are evaluated over the same Library.
content.interpretation: Changing the reference may alter the observer-relative accessibility relation, but it does not alter the underlying totality.

content.text: No configuration is privileged as the universal starting point of coherent traversal. If x and x' are both admissible observer-relative reference configurations, changing the reference changes the relational evaluation without changing Library membership. A privileged construction origin would introduce an asymmetry into traversal that is not present in the foundational ontology.

Reference-point neutrality does not, by itself, prove that every possible reference admits a coherent continuation. The stronger requirement must therefore be stated explicitly. The model requires that every admissible observer-relative reference configuration remain capable of at least one coherent continuation for every compatible observer and history.

content.title: Reference-Point Coherence Proposition
content.text: Every admissible observer-relative reference configuration must admit at least one coherent continuation under the observer and history compatible with that reference.
content.latex: \forall x \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{admissible}},\ \forall(O,h)\text{ compatible with }x,\ \exists \gamma \in \operatorname{Path}(\mathcal{M}): \gamma\text{ begins at }(h,x) \land \mathcal{C}(\gamma \mid O,h,x)=1
content.interpretation: This is a derived model requirement arising from the combined requirements of maximal static totality, reference-point neutrality, whole-Library relationality, and continued coherent traversal from arbitrary admissible references. It is not claimed to follow from maximality alone.

content.text: The proposition therefore does not say that every path from every configuration is coherent. It says only that an admissible reference cannot be a dead end solely because of its location in the Library. Coherent traversal must remain possible without introducing a privileged origin or an observer-independent boundary.

content.title: Observer-Relative Accessibility
content.text: Accessibility from an admissible reference is defined over the unchanged Library.
content.latex: A_O(h,x) = \{y \in \mathcal{M} \mid \exists \gamma \in \operatorname{Path}(\mathcal{M})\text{ beginning at }(h,x)\text{ and containing }y\text{ such that }\mathcal{C}(\gamma \mid O,h,x)=1\}
content.interpretation: The accessible subset emerges from the relation between the observer, its history, its reference, and the static Library.

content.text: The resulting construction is explicitly non-idealistic. The observer does not create A_O(h,x) as new ontology. Rather, A_O(h,x) is a subset relation over configurations already contained in 𝓜. Likewise, a configuration outside A_O(h,x) remains a member of 𝓜 unless independently excluded by the formal characterization of the Library.

The same distinction permits domain-neutral application. A physical observer may access a subset of physical configurations; an AI system may access a subset of a knowledge or reasoning domain; a financial observer may access a subset of actionable market states. In each case the formal relation is unchanged: accessibility is determined relative to an observer, its current relational conditions, and the coherent continuations available within the underlying totality.

The observer's reference therefore functions as a relational anchor rather than a privileged origin. Moving the reference from x to x' can alter which configurations are accessible through coherent traversal, but it cannot alter 𝓜 itself. This is the required separation between observer-relative worldline structure and Library ontology.

content.setup: Suppose x and y are both configurations in the unchanged Library 𝓜, with x ∈ 𝓜_admissible. Assume there exists a path γ_x beginning from (h,x) such that 𝓒(γ_x | O,h,x)=1, while no currently accessible O-coherent path from (h,x) contains y.
content.result: Then x ∈ 𝓜, y ∈ 𝓜, y ∉ A_O(h,x), and a coherent continuation from x remains available.
content.interpretation: The example demonstrates that accessibility is not existence. The observer's traversal from x identifies a restricted relational subset of the unchanged totality; it does not generate that subset as new ontology. Likewise, inability to access y does not remove y from 𝓜.

content.setup: Let x_1 and x_2 be two admissible reference configurations in 𝓜.
content.result: The observer-relative accessibility relations A_O(h,x_1) and A_O(h,x_2) may differ, while the underlying Library remains 𝓜 in both cases.
content.interpretation: Neither reference is a privileged universal origin. The difference belongs to the observer-relative traversal relation rather than to the ontology of the Library.

content.text: No intrinsic past/future partition is introduced into 𝓜 by this construction. The sequence of configurations encountered by an observer constitutes an ordering relative to its history and reference. Apparent temporal and complexity ordering therefore belongs to observer-relative traversal rather than to evolution of the Library itself.

The formal boundary is consequently narrow. This subsection establishes accessibility, reference-point neutrality, and the requirement of coherent continuation from admissible references. It does not yet introduce emergent physical law, probabilistic dynamics, consciousness, physical time, or cosmological interpretation.

subsections.title: Observer-Relative Reality
subsections.content:
Experienced reality is defined here as the subset of the Library that is accessible to a particular observer through a coherent path. For observer O, we therefore define experienced reality as R_O := A_O, where A_O is the observer-accessible subset established in the preceding section. This definition does not assert that the observer creates the accessible configurations. It states only that the configurations available through observer-relative coherent traversal constitute that observer's experienced reality. The ontological domain remains the Library 𝓜, while experienced reality is a subset of that domain. Because the resolution threshold I_N(O) is observer-relative, there is no requirement that all observers have identical accessible subsets. Let the collection of observers be Obs = {O_1,O_2,...}. For each observer O_i, the corresponding experienced reality is R_i = A_{O_i}. Two observers may therefore traverse overlapping but non-identical regions of the Library. This difference follows from the relational construction of distinguishability and coherence: what remains resolvable and coherently traversable for one observer need not be identical to what remains resolvable and coherently traversable for another. The common portion of two observer-relative realities is represented by their intersection: \[
R_{ij} = R_i \cap R_j.
\] The set R_{ij} contains configurations accessible to both observers. A non-empty intersection therefore provides a formal basis for shared reality without requiring the two observers to possess identical accessible domains. Conversely, the observer-relative difference between their accessible realities can be represented by the symmetric difference: \[
D_{ij} = R_i \triangle R_j.
\] The set D_{ij} contains configurations accessible to one observer but not the other. Such a difference should not be interpreted as evidence that the observers inhabit mutually incompatible ontological universes. Both R_i and R_j remain subsets of the same Library 𝓜: \[
R_i \subseteq \mathcal{M}, \qquad R_j \subseteq \mathcal{M}.
\] Thus, observer-relative reality describes a difference in access, resolution, and coherent survivability rather than a difference in fundamental existence. A configuration may belong to 𝓜 while being inaccessible to one observer, accessible to another, or accessible to both. Inaccessibility therefore remains a relational property and does not constitute ontological erasure. This distinction also prevents observer-relative reality from collapsing into a claim of arbitrary subjectivity. The observer does not freely select an arbitrary reality. Accessibility is constrained by the formal structure of 𝓜, the observer's distinguishability relation δ_O, the observer-relative threshold I_N(O), and the requirement that coherent paths remain resolvable. Different observers may consequently obtain different accessible subsets while still sharing substantial structure because their coherent path spaces overlap within the same underlying Library. The construction can therefore be summarized as follows: the Library specifies the total formal configuration domain; each observer induces an observer-relative accessibility relation over that domain; and experienced reality is the resulting accessible subset. Reality is observer-relative at the level of access, but not thereby observer-created at the level of ontology.

mathematics.interpretation: R_{ij} represents shared accessible structure, while D_{ij} represents observer-relative difference in accessibility.

The metaphor therefore compresses the distinction between observer-relative access and underlying ontological membership without introducing a competing ontology.

section.purpose: Explain how law-like regularity can arise through observer-relative survivorship without being imposed as an axiom.
